title: Roberto:
headline: Inside detention they hand you a list of law firms. Most never answer. AIJ always did.
story: Inside detention you cannot even get a glass of cold water. They give you a list of law firms. Most never pick up.
Americans for Immigrant Justice always answered, and then said: “Come, we will represent you.” Now he is free. The spine is “they always answered”, not a list of complaints.

transcript:
Roberto Client Interview.mp4. English translation by AIJ (Translation with notes from Andres.docx). Times are the transcript's block markers, not frame-exact. Speaker 1 = Andres (interviewer), Speaker 2 = Roberto. Only the blocks these cuts use are here.
[00:56] Speaker 2: Um, I would like to share part of my story; how my immigration process was like in this country, um, how Americans for Immigrant Justice, um, lent me a helping hand, with a lot of - of support in this immigration process, while I was in a detention center in Miami - Krome in Miami...and a bit more about that.
[01:37] Speaker 2: Um, well, I would mainly like to send out, well, a message, because this message is especially for people, or...um, their family members, who are currently in a situation like the one I went through, since right now, the immigration situation in this country is a bit rigorous. So, this message is especially for all those people, and it's to not give up and to keep knocking on doors, because there are always people and foundations, or companies, like Americans for Immigrant Justice, who are willing to lend a helping hand in some way. [...do not use: arrest history, about 02:00-04:00...]
[~04:00] After I moved to Orlando, I went and reported to the ICE appointment, which was in January 2025, and I was aand I had a pending asylum case. I showed them that I had my license, that I had no criminal convictions, but I was still arrested [...] little did I know then that I was going to spend a year at the Krome Detention Center in Miami. Um, really, I never considered - never considered going back to Colombia because my situation in Colombia is delicated, given the violence from armed gangs and problems that my family has gone through, with family members who were dismembered and have gone missing.
[05:37] So, because of that, I painfully made the decision. [...] so I made the decision to continue with my immigration case inside the detention center, and it lasted for a year. During that year, I met Americans for Immigration Justice, who gave me very essential support at all times. They prepared me, gave me hope and a sigh of relief, and were by my side the entire time. And - and to my surprise, my asylum was approved in
[06:37] 2025 in October of 20 - sorry. On October 30, 2025, my asylum was approved, because I had God's blessing and Americans for Immigrant Justice's support, who sincerely did an excellent job.
[07:02] Speaker 1 asks him to move the phone so his head sits higher in the frame.
[08:06] Speaker 2: Umm, well, um, what I can say, since it's common knowledge, is that Colombia is a country, a country that has always been ruled by a drug - it's a narco-state, so a lot of criminal groups have been created, which operate outside the law, affecting some sectors and several parts of Colombia, and they suff - the civilian population is the one that is worst off in this situation. They face hostility - a high risk of hostility from - through the use of powerful weapons, forced displacement, people going missing, murders, dismemberments, and bodies of murder victims in full view of us. So, it's something that led us to raise our voices, and for doing so,
[09:06] our lives were always at risk, and for that decis - for that reason, I made the decision to seek asylum in this country.
[09:46] Speaker 2: Well the word to immigrate is a synonym for several things that can't be described with just one word. Sometimes we make the decision to leave our country, not because of money, but rather, because we don't have peace, we don't have a safe place, so we need to leave our families behind. Well that, to me, has been one of the saddest situations I have experienced, because it was either keep living that way, or be without them for the rest of my life, or risk my own life. So, it's something that's sad, and simply put, people that have gone through that are the ones that truly understand the circumstances.
[13:16] Speaker 2: Umm. Well, um, honestly, the truth is, they gave us a - a - a document that had um - um...the contact information of law firms, who could represent us at no cost or also for - for an added cost. So, we would try, but during that time, the whole situation was very difficult; several of those law firms would not answer. Others wouldn't answer, but Americans for Immigrants is one of those who always did, um. I honestly don't know how they did it, but they did a very good job. They were always there, they always answered, even when, um, several times, I was denied the opportunity to be represented by them, since it was - was free legal representation.
[14:16] But I insisted, and insisted, and insisted, and they finally decided to represent me, once they saw that it had been 7 months and that I was still not deported. They said: "No, come, we will represent you." They represented me and did their best, because now, here I am outside of detention; I'm free and thank God my case was approved and thanks to them for their excellent work. My message is: to everyone, um, who is currently going through this process, leave this type of work to people like them. Honestly, we think we know a lot of things or we rush to make decisions, but really, we don't know anything. So, it's important to have guidance from a - from people, um, who know about the matter, subject matter experts like Americans for Immigrant Justice, who honestly, to me, they have highly valuable expertise.
[23:15] Speaker 2: [...] So, we should not stop supporting one another and keep fighting, so that those people in those situations could know their worth or their rights, um, and to - to - to more united in that situation, because honestly, um...you could never imagine what it's like being locked up, or that you would like to drink a - of cold water and you can't - you can't even drink a glass of cold water. [...]
[25:34] Speaker 2: E - exactly. My experience with Americans for Immigrant Justice was that they always had people who spoke to me in Spanish, who had the time to talk to me, because honestly, when you are there, you don't...you have time, time to spare, and you don't know how it's like outside, but Americans for Immigrant Justice always had time to explain to me, to give me that, like, hope. So, that's why it's very important for me that...I don't know where the funding comes from, however they get it, I don't know how that's done...but it's very important that [Americans for Immigrant Justice] remains or that it withstands, for the people who truly deserve it, because we know that there are also people who come with one idea or those that get lost in other ideas, and they do
[26:34] bad things. So, it's very important that you all keep doing the work that you do because there are people who truly need it.
[26:44] Speaker 1: (do not use anything after this point)
